en: The last important piece I want to dive in
here is the memory feature, because that's
another quite common building block you'll
see in some agents, especially those generic
agents. And the idea behind memory is that
maybe you want your agent to memorize
certain pieces of information across
sessions. Because by default, whenever you
start a new session, all the previous
information from another session is lost.
Every session gets this fresh context
window, which has a bunch of invisible stuff
loaded into it. You learned about that. But
which does not know anything about other
sessions. But many general agents like
Claude Cowork do indeed have a built-in
memory feature. And we saw that here earlier
already because I already, well,
did some data analysis tasks or sessions
here. And in one of those sessions, I told
it to remember something, that it should
always output 2 key KPIs in the final
response.
And it then
updated its memory again, because that is a
feature built into Claude Cowork.
It has a built-in memory feature. Now, if
you were working with an agent that doesn't
have it, you can still kind of replicate it
by, for example, telling it that it stores
some information in a markdown file
in a folder named memory or whatever name
you want.
And by then telling it, or by manually doing
it, that in the Claude or agents.md file,
depending on which agent you're using,
you want an instruction that this memory
folder must always be analyzed and the files
in there must always be read. And that then
gives the agent a dynamic way of manually
managing a memory and ensuring that it's
always getting loaded whenever a new session
starts, because Claude and AgentsMD are
always loaded when a new session starts. And
if you have an instruction in there that
tells the agent to load the memory, that
effectively also gets always loaded when a
new session starts. And that's a way how you
could rebuild such a memory. Feature in case
your agent, your agent harness doesn't have
it built in. But again, as the developer of
an agent, that's also something you have to
actively build. And here again is this
task-specific agent I've been showing you
over and over again, which we will explore
in greater detail later. But I can tell you
this agent does not have a memory feature
because it doesn't need it. And you couldn't
even replicate this manual memory storage
because it has no read or write file tools
because again, for its tasks, it doesn't
need it. And that's really just one of the
key takeaways here. These are building
blocks you can, but don't necessarily have
to support when building an agent. It
depends on what your agent should be doing.
As a user of an agent, especially as a user
of a general agent,
you most of the time can use these different
building blocks because most general agents
do support them. But for some features, you
can also work around missing capabilities if
you need to. And with that, we had a
thorough look at core building blocks and
context engineering and what you should
consider when it comes to steering and
controlling an agent and most importantly,
its context window, both from the
perspective of a user as well as a potential
developer of an agent.
